vignette:
He remembers the day exactly—April 14, 2019. A Tuesday. He was on a maintenance call at a small commercial bakery, working alone to replace a corroded compressor in a rooftop HVAC unit. The unit was old, its refrigerant lines caked with rust and unidentified sludge. He had his standard safety gear: gloves, goggles, a dust mask. Not a respirator. The company didn’t require one for routine service, and he’d done this kind of work for twenty-three years without a problem.

The leak happened when he loosened a fitting. A sudden, hissing cloud of yellowish gas shot into his face before he could turn away. He choked, stumbled backward, felt his eyes burn and his throat close. He scrambled down the ladder, coughing violently, gasping for clean air. The bakery manager called 911. An ambulance took him to the ER, where they gave him oxygen and monitored his lungs. The chemical turned out to be a mix of old R-22 refrigerant and decomposed lubricant that had been heated and pressurized. The doctors said he was lucky—no permanent lung damage, just acute irritation. He was discharged that evening with an inhaler and a warning to be more careful.

He went back to work three days later. He told himself it was nothing. But the smell of the bakery—yeast, warm sugar, exhaust from the ovens—made his stomach turn. He finished the job with a tight chest and a pounding heart. Over the next few weeks, he started noticing things. The hum of a compressor would make him freeze. The sight of a yellowed label on a refrigerant tank would send a cold rush down his spine. He began to avoid calls that involved older units. He made excuses: back pain, schedule conflicts. His supervisor noticed and started assigning him easier jobs, which made him feel useless and ashamed.

At home, his wife noticed the changes first. He stopped sleeping through the night. He’d lie awake replaying the moment the gas hit his face, the burning in his throat, the helplessness of not being able to breathe. Sometimes he’d jerk awake, gasping, convinced he was back on the roof. He stopped going to family gatherings. The smell of grilled meat reminded him of the bakery. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a dropped pan—made him duck. He found himself checking his equipment obsessively, even when he wasn’t working. He’d test his safety gear twice, three times, still not sure it was enough.

He began to carry a small inhaler in his pocket, even though his lungs had cleared. He felt a constant knot in his stomach, a low-grade dread that never quite left. He avoided the freeway exit that led to the bakery. He stopped watching the news when a story about an industrial accident came on. His wife tried to talk to him, but he’d shrug and say he was fine, just tired. He didn’t know how to explain the images that flashed behind his eyes—the yellow cloud, the taste of metal, the feeling of the world going dim.

Today, three years later, he still works as an HVAC technician, but he has a permanent note in his file: no rooftop work, no units over ten years old. He does mostly residential furnace tune-ups, which feels like a demotion. He keeps his back to the door in any room. He cannot tolerate the smell of burnt dust. He has not had a full night’s sleep in months. He still wakes up gasping, his hands reaching for a mask that isn’t there.
